title: Capacitance & Capacitors
summary: A capacitor stores charge and energy in an electric field. Its capacitance is $C = Q/V$ (farads). For parallel plates $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$, energy stored is $U = \tfrac12 C V^2$, a dielectric multiplies $C$ by $\kappa$, and capacitors combine in series and parallel. (University Physics Vol. 2, Ch. 8.)

concept_sections.heading: What a capacitor does
concept_sections.explanation: A capacitor is two conductors holding equal and opposite charge $\pm Q$, separated by an insulator. It stores charge (and energy) when a voltage is applied. Capacitance measures how much charge it holds per volt: $C = Q/V$, in farads (1 F = 1 C/V). A farad is huge, so real capacitors are µF, nF, or pF.

figure.caption: Two conductors hold $\pm Q$; capacitance is the charge stored per volt, $C = Q/V$.

concept_sections.heading: Parallel-plate capacitor
concept_sections.explanation: For two flat plates of area $A$ separated by $d$ (vacuum), $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$. Bigger plates or a smaller gap store more charge per volt. This shows capacitance is set by geometry, not by how much charge you happen to put on it.

figure.caption: Capacitance grows with plate area $A$ and shrinks with gap $d$: $C = \varepsilon_0 A/d$.

concept_sections.heading: Energy stored
concept_sections.explanation: Charging a capacitor stores energy in its field: $U = \tfrac12 C V^2 = \tfrac12 Q V = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C}$. These three forms are equal; pick whichever fits the quantities you know. This energy can be released quickly — the idea behind a camera flash.

figure.caption: Charging stores energy in the field between the plates: $U = \tfrac12 CV^2 = \tfrac12 QV = Q^2/2C$.

concept_sections.heading: Dielectrics
concept_sections.explanation: Filling the gap with an insulating dielectric increases capacitance by the dielectric constant $\kappa$: $C = \dfrac{\kappa \varepsilon_0 A}{d}$. The dielectric partly cancels the field, letting the plates hold more charge at the same voltage. Typical $\kappa$: paper $\approx 3$, water $\approx 80$.

figure.caption: A dielectric's aligned molecules partly cancel the field, raising capacitance to $C = \kappa\varepsilon_0 A/d$.

concept_sections.heading: Combining capacitors
concept_sections.explanation: In parallel the plates share the voltage and capacitances add: $C_{eq} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots$. In series the charge is the same on each and reciprocals add: $\dfrac{1}{C_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \cdots$, so the series total is smaller than any single capacitor.

figure.caption: Parallel capacitances add; in series the reciprocals add (the total is smaller).

real_world_examples.title: Camera flash
real_world_examples.scenario: A camera charges up, then fires a bright flash.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: A capacitor slowly stores energy $U = \tfrac12 CV^2$, then dumps it into the flash tube in milliseconds for a burst of light.

figure.caption: The capacitor stores $U = \tfrac12 CV^2$ slowly, then releases it to the flash tube in milliseconds.

real_world_examples.title: Computer memory (DRAM)
real_world_examples.scenario: Each bit of DRAM is a tiny capacitor.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Charged ($Q=CV$) means '1', uncharged means '0'. Because $C$ is tiny it leaks and must be refreshed thousands of times a second.

figure.caption: Each DRAM bit is a tiny capacitor: charged ($Q=CV$) is 1, empty is 0 — it leaks and must be refreshed.

real_world_examples.title: Touchscreen
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Your finger changes the local capacitance $C = \kappa\varepsilon_0 A/d$ of the screen grid; the device detects that change to locate the touch.

figure.caption: A fingertip alters the local capacitance $C=\kappa\varepsilon_0 A/d$ of the screen grid, locating the touch.

problems.prompt: A capacitor holds $6.0\ \mu\text{C}$ at $12$ V. Find its capacitance.
A $10\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is connected to $9.0$ V. How much charge does it store?
Find the energy stored in a $100\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $50$ V.
Parallel plates have area $A = 0.020\ \text{m}^2$ and gap $d = 1.0$ mm (vacuum). Find $C$.
A $2.0\ \mu\text{F}$ vacuum capacitor is filled with a dielectric of $\kappa = 3.0$. Find the new capacitance.
Capacitors of $2$, $4$, and $6\ \mu\text{F}$ are connected in parallel. Find the equivalent capacitance.
A $6.0\ \mu\text{F}$ and a $3.0\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor are in series. Find the equivalent capacitance.
problems.hint: In series, add reciprocals; the total is smaller than either.

problems.prompt: A $20\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is charged to $200$ V. Find the charge and the energy stored.
A $3.0\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is in parallel with a series pair of two $6.0\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitors. Find the total capacitance.
problems.hint: Reduce the series pair first, then add the parallel capacitor.

problems.prompt: A $5.0\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is charged to $100$ V and then disconnected from the battery. A dielectric with $\kappa = 2.0$ is inserted. Find the new voltage and stored energy.
solution_steps: Disconnected means $Q$ is fixed: $Q = CV = (5.0\times10^{-6})(100) = 5.0\times10^{-4}$ C.
New capacitance $C' = \kappa C = 10\ \mu$F, so $V' = Q/C' = \dfrac{5.0\times10^{-4}}{10\times10^{-6}} = 50$ V.
problems.hint: With the battery removed the charge stays constant while $C$ doubles.
